title: What do the 2025 Standards for RTOs require of training and assessment?
description: What the 2025 Standards for RTOs require of training, assessment, validation, RPL and trainer credentials, with clause references and evidence to keep.
shortAnswer: The 2025 Standards for Registered Training Organisations (RTOs), in force since 1 July 2025, require training that is consistent with the training product, informed by industry, and paced for practice and feedback. Assessment must follow the principles of assessment and rules of evidence, tools must be reviewed before use, and every training product must be validated at least once every five years by credentialled people.
keyTakeaways: The 2025 Standards for RTOs commenced on 1 July 2025 and replaced the Standards for RTOs 2015 for RTOs regulated by the Australian Skills Quality Authority (ASQA).
They have three parts: the Outcome Standards, the Compliance Standards (with the Fit and Proper Person Requirements), and the Credential Policy.
Quality Area 1 (Standards 1.1 to 1.8) covers training, industry engagement, assessment systems, validation, recognition of prior learning, credit transfer, and resources.
Assessment tools must be reviewed before use, and every training product must be validated at least once every five years, more often when risks or changes arise.

Only people holding a training and assessment or assessment only credential listed in Sections 1A and 1B of the Credential Policy, such as TAE40122, may make assessment judgments; others work under direction.
appliesTo: Registered training organisations regulated by ASQA
Enterprise RTOs delivering nationally recognised training to their own workforce
Trainers, assessors, and validators working for or on behalf of an RTO
Third parties delivering training or assessment on behalf of an RTO

sections.heading: What are the 2025 Standards for RTOs?

blocks.text: The 2025 Standards for RTOs are the national quality rules that Registered Training Organisations must meet to deliver nationally recognized vocational education and training (VET). As at September 2026, they have been in force since 1 July 2025, and [ASQA states](https://www.asqa.gov.au/for-providers/standards-for-RTOs/about-the-standards) that they have three components: the Outcome Standards, the Compliance Standards, and the Credential Policy.

The legally binding documents are the [National Vocational Education and Training Regulator (Outcome Standards for Registered Training Organisations) Instrument 2025](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L00354/asmade/text) and the [National Vocational Education and Training Regulator (Compliance Standards for NVR Registered Training Organisations and Fit and Proper Person Requirements) Instrument 2025](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L00355/asmade/text). Both were made under the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Act 2011, registered on 14 March 2025, and commenced on 1 July 2025. Schedule 3 of the Compliance Standards instrument repeals the Standards for Registered Training Organisations (RTOs) 2015. The [Credential Policy](https://content.training.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-03/Credential%20Policy.pdf) is published on the National Register (training.gov.au) and incorporated by reference.

The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations (DEWR) explains that the split was deliberate: compliance and administrative requirements were moved out of the Outcome Standards so that the Outcome Standards focus on learner outcomes ([DEWR FAQ](https://www.dewr.gov.au/standards-for-rtos/revised-standards-rtos-frequently-asked-questions)). DEWR also publishes policy documents in a more readable format, but notes that those policy documents do not impose legal obligations. The instruments do.

sections.heading: Who do the 2025 Standards apply to?

blocks.text: The 2025 Standards apply to every RTO regulated by ASQA, the National VET Regulator. According to [DEWR](https://www.dewr.gov.au/standards-for-rtos), RTOs regulated only by the Training Accreditation Council (TAC) in Western Australia or the Victorian Registration and Qualifications Authority (VRQA) follow state legislation and should confirm their obligations with that regulator.

For regulated employers this matters in two ways. Enterprise RTOs that train their own staff must meet the Standards in full. Organizations that buy accredited training from an RTO, for example a Certificate IV in a regulated occupation, can use the Standards as a checklist when they select and audit providers, because the RTO's obligations extend to third parties that deliver training or assessment on its behalf.

Quality Area 1 of the Outcome Standards is titled Training and assessment and contains eight standards across four divisions. Its outcome statement reads: "quality training and assessment engages VET students and enables them to attain nationally recognised, industry-relevant competencies" ([Outcome Standards, Schedule 1](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L00354/asmade/text)).

sections.heading: What do the Standards require of training delivery?

blocks.text: Standard 1.1 requires training to be consistent with the training product and structured so that students can actually reach the required competency. Its performance indicators include that "training is structured and paced to support VET students to progress, providing sufficient time for instruction, practice, feedback and assessment".

The same standard requires modes of delivery that enable students to attain the skills and knowledge in the training product, and training techniques and resources that engage students. Where a training product requires work placement, the RTO must show the necessary skills and knowledge can be attained in that environment. Standard 1.2 adds that the RTO must demonstrate how it identifies relevant industry, employer, and community representatives, how it uses their advice to change training and assessment strategies, and that "training reflects current industry practice".

In practice this means the design logic of a course has to be visible. A unit of competency in a training package sets out performance criteria, knowledge evidence, and assessment conditions; the RTO's learning activities, time allocations, and resources should trace back to them. This is the same discipline described in [competency-based training](/glossary/competency-based-training) and in writing [measurable learning outcomes](/guides/how-to-write-measurable-learning-outcomes).

sections.heading: What do the Standards require of assessment?

blocks.text: Standards 1.3 and 1.4 require an assessment system that is consistent with the training product and produces accurate judgments of competency. Assessment tools must be "reviewed prior to use" to confirm they can be used in line with the principles of assessment and rules of evidence, and the results of those reviews must inform changes to the tools.

Standard 1.4 sets out four principles of assessment and four rules of evidence. The principles are fairness (including reasonable adjustments and reassessment), flexibility, validity, and reliability. Notably, the validity principle now states that assessment "includes practical application components that enable the VET student to demonstrate the relevant skills and knowledge in a practical setting". The rules of evidence are validity, sufficiency, authenticity, and currency, and each assessor's individual judgment must be justified against them.

The instrument defines an assessment tool as including the context and conditions of assessment, the tasks, an outline of the evidence to be gathered, the criteria used to judge competency, and the administration, recording, and reporting requirements. An [assessment blueprint](/glossary/assessment-blueprint) that maps each task to the unit requirements is a practical way to show this before a tool is used; see also [how to design competency assessments](/guides/how-to-design-competency-assessments).

Records matter too. Section 10 of the [Compliance Standards](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L00355/asmade/text) requires RTOs to retain records of all assessments submitted by a student for 2 years after the student completes the training product, and records of AQF certification documentation for thirty years.

sections.heading: How often must assessment be validated, and by whom?

blocks.text: Under Standard 1.5, every training product on an RTO's scope of registration must be validated at least once every five years, and more often where the RTO becomes aware of risks to training outcomes, changes to the training product, or relevant feedback from students, trainers, assessors, or industry. The RTO decides which parts of the assessment system to validate, and the sample size, using a risk based approach.

items: The people validating must collectively have relevant industry competencies, a practical understanding of current industry practice, and one of the validation credentials listed in the Credential Policy.
The outcome of a validation must not be solely determined by a person who designed or delivered the training or assessment.
The RTO must show how validation outcomes are used to change the assessment system.

For Training and Education (TAE) Training Package qualifications or skill sets that let people make assessment judgments, an additional independent validation is required once the first cohort completes.

blocks.text: Section 3A of the [Credential Policy](https://content.training.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-03/Credential%20Policy.pdf) lists the validation credentials for non TAE products, including TAE40122, TAE40116, and TAE40110 Certificate IV in Training and Assessment, the TAESS00019, TAESS00011, and TAESS00001 Assessor Skill Sets, and a diploma or higher level qualification in adult education or VET.

sections.heading: What do the Standards say about recognition of prior learning and credit transfer?

blocks.text: Standards 1.6 and 1.7 require RTOs to offer students the opportunity to seek [recognition of prior learning](/glossary/recognition-of-prior-learning) (RPL) and credit transfer, and to make them aware of the relevant policies. RPL decisions must be based on evidence of prior skills, learning, and experience and made through the RTO's assessment system.

Credit transfer decisions must be based on AQF certification documentation or an authenticated VET transcript, unless licensing or regulatory requirements prevent it. For both, decisions must be documented and made in a way that is fair, transparent, consistent between students, and maintains the integrity of the training product. For workforce programs, this is where an existing competency record is worth having: it becomes the evidence base for RPL rather than a list of attendance dates.

sections.heading: What credentials do trainers and assessors need?

blocks.text: Standard 3.2 requires that training and assessment is "only delivered by persons who hold the appropriate credentials for the delivery of training and assessment as specified in the Credential Policy". Standard 3.3 separately requires industry competencies at least to the level of the training product being delivered or assessed, and an understanding of current industry practice.

blocks.text: Delivering TAE qualifications themselves carries higher requirements under Section 2: for example, delivering TAE40122 or the TAESS00019 Assessor Skill Set requires a Diploma of Vocational Education and Training (such as TAE50122) or equivalent listed credential. DEWR notes that holders of the older TAE40110 no longer need the two additional units previously required. All trainers and assessors must also undertake continuing professional development in training and assessment under Standard 3.2.

sections.heading: What evidence shows each requirement is met?

blocks.text: ASQA says the 2025 Standards give providers more flexibility in how they demonstrate that they meet them ([ASQA](https://www.asqa.gov.au/newsroom/latest-news/2025-standards-rtos-commence)), so the evidence is the RTO's to design. The table below is an original mapping, not ASQA guidance, of what to build and what to keep for each training and assessment requirement.

blocks.title: Transition point
blocks.text: Policies, tool templates, and audit checklists written against the 2015 Standards cite a clause numbering that no longer applies. Standard 1.8, for example, now covers facilities, resources and equipment. Update every internal reference to the 2025 instruments and the Credential Policy.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models the unit requirements, learning outcomes, and assessment points as a structured framework before content is written, so each activity and assessment task has a traceable link to the training product. That link is what an RTO needs to show consistency under Standards 1.1 and 1.3 and to scope validation under Standard 1.5. See [educational programs](/programs/educational) and the related page on [AQF levels and learning outcomes](/regulations/aqf-levels-and-learning-outcomes).

faqs.q: When did the 2025 Standards for RTOs start?
faqs.a: They commenced on 1 July 2025. Both legislative instruments were registered on the Federal Register of Legislation on 14 March 2025, and the Compliance Standards instrument repealed the Standards for RTOs 2015 from the same date. As at September 2026 the Outcome Standards instrument remains in force as made.

faqs.q: Do the 2025 Standards apply in Victoria and Western Australia?
faqs.a: They apply to all RTOs regulated by ASQA, including ASQA regulated RTOs operating in Victoria and Western Australia. RTOs registered only with the VRQA or TAC WA follow state legislation and regulator requirements, and DEWR advises those RTOs to check with their regulator.

faqs.q: Can someone without a Certificate IV in Training and Assessment deliver training?
faqs.a: Yes, under direction. The Credential Policy allows people actively working toward TAE40122 or TAE50122, or holding listed skill sets or a secondary teaching qualification, to deliver training and contribute to assessment under the direction of a fully credentialled trainer. They cannot make assessment judgments.

faqs.q: Are ASQA practice guides legally binding?
faqs.a: No. ASQA practice guides describe ASQA's regulatory expectations, examples of compliance, and self assurance questions, but the obligations sit in the two legislative instruments and the Credential Policy. Similarly, DEWR states that its policy document versions of the Standards do not impose legal obligations.

faqs.q: How does this relate to higher education standards?
faqs.a: The 2025 Standards govern VET delivered by RTOs. Higher education providers are regulated by the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency against the Higher Education Standards Framework. Dual sector providers must meet both; see the page on [TEQSA HESF course design requirements](/regulations/teqsa-hesf-course-design-requirements).

factCheck.claim: The Outcome Standards instrument and the Compliance Standards instrument each commence on 1 July 2025 (section 2), were registered on 14 March 2025, and are made under the National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Act 2011.

Schedule 3 of the Compliance Standards instrument repeals the Standards for Registered Training Organisations (RTOs) 2015; section 10 requires assessment records to be retained for 2 years after completion and AQF certification records for thirty years.

Quality Area 1 contains Standards 1.1 to 1.8 in four divisions (Training; Assessment; Recognition of prior learning and credit transfer; Facilities, resources and equipment); Standard 1.3(2)(b) requires assessment tools to be reviewed prior to use; Standard 1.4 sets out principles of assessment and rules of evidence, with validity including practical application components.

Standard 1.5(2)(b) requires every training product on scope to be validated at least once every five years and more often on risk, change, or feedback; 1.5(2)(f) says the outcome must not be solely determined by a person who designed or delivered the training or assessment.

Standard 3.2(2)(a) requires training and assessment to be delivered only by persons holding credentials specified in the Credential Policy; Standard 3.3 requires industry competencies at least to the level of the training product.

Credential Policy Section 1A lists TAE40122, TAE40116, TAE40110, a diploma or higher qualification in adult education or VET, or a secondary teaching qualification with TAESS00011, TAESS00019 or TAESS00024; Section 1C requires completion of TAE40122 or TAE50122 within two years of commencement; Section 3A lists validation credentials.
ASQA states the 2025 Standards came into effect on 1 July 2025 and have three components: Outcome Standards, Compliance Standards, and Credential Policy.
DEWR states RTOs regulated by TAC WA and VRQA follow state legislation, that policy documents do not impose legal obligations, and that TAE40110 holders no longer need the two additional units.
